hook.line: Everyone asks how the weekend went. *Fue bien* is flat; Spanish has a little phrase for the whole experience, whether it was great or terrible.
hook.en: Did you have a good time at the party? (to a friend)

examples.en: Did you have a good time at the party? (to a friend)

examples.es: La pasé muy mal cuando nos separamos.
examples.en: I had a really hard time when we split up.
We had a wonderful time at the farm!

examples.es: Vale la pasó genial en Medellín.
examples.en: Vale had a great time in Medellín.

examples.es: Ayer la pasamos horrible con el tráfico.
examples.en: Yesterday we had a horrible time with the traffic.
How did you all have it in Cartagena? (you all)

rule:
*Pasar* is *to spend*. *La pasé bien* means *I spent it well*: *la* stands for the time itself (*la vida*, *la fiesta*, *la semana*), and it is always *la*, whatever the person.

*La pasé*, *la pasaste*, *la pasó*, *la pasamos*, *la pasaron*

Add the verdict: *bien*, *mal*, *genial*, *horrible*, *delicioso* (very Colombian for a great time). *Muy* turns it up.

It reports a whole stretch of time, not one fact. It is casual, perfect with friends.
smallPrint: Teachers call this an idiom with a feminine *la* that refers to nothing in particular.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *la* or *lo* and type the whole sentence: *¿___ pasaste bien en la fiesta?* (Did you have a good time at the party? To a friend.)
yourTurn.why: It is always *la*: it stands for the time you spent.

yourTurn.why: *La pasamos* for we, plus the Colombian *delicioso*.

pitfalls.right: La pasé bien en la fiesta.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Without *la* it sounds like you walked past something.
*Lo pasé* is what people say in Spain; in Latin America it's *la pasé*.
After the verb you need an adverb: *bien*, not *bueno*.

personal: Think of your last weekend. Say how it went: *La pasé...* plus *bien*, *mal*, *genial* or *horrible*.
